{{short description|Algebraic structure with a ternary operation}}
In [[abstract algebra]], a '''semiheap''' is an [[algebraic structure]] consisting of a [[empty set|non-empty]] [[set (mathematics)|set]] {{mvar|H}} with a [[ternary operation]] denoted <math>[x,y,z] \in H</math> that satisfies a modified associativity property:<ref name="H&L"/>{{rp|56}}
<math display="block">\forall a,b,c,d,e \in H \quad [[a,b,c],d,e] = [a,[d,c,b],e] = [a,b,[c,d,e]].</math>

A '''biunitary element''' {{mvar|h}} of a semiheap satisfies {{math|1=[''h'',''h'',''k''] = ''k'' = [''k'',''h'',''h'']}} for every {{mvar|k}} in {{mvar|H}}.<ref name="H&L"/>{{rp|75,6}}

A '''heap''' is a semiheap in which every element is biunitary.<ref name="H&L"/>{{rp|80}} It can be thought of as a [[group_(mathematics)|group]] with the identity element "forgotten".

The term ''heap'' is derived from {{lang|ru|груда}}, Russian for {{gloss|heap}} or {{gloss|pile}}. [[Anton Sushkevich]] used the term in his ''Theory of Generalized Groups'' (1937) which influenced [[Viktor Wagner]], promulgator of semiheaps, heaps, and generalized heaps.<ref name=H&L>C.D. Hollings & M.V. Lawson (2017) ''Wagner's Theory of Generalised Heaps'', [[Springer books]] {{ISBN|978-3-319-63620-7}} {{mr|id=3729305}}</ref>{{rp|11}} {{lang|ru|Груда}} contrasts with {{lang|ru|группа}} ([[group (mathematics)|group]]) which was taken into Russian by transliteration. Indeed, a heap has been called a '''groud''' in English text.<ref>Schein (1979) pp.101–102: footnote (o)</ref>

==Examples==

=== Two element heap ===
Turn <math>H=\{a,b\}</math> into the [[cyclic group]] <math>\mathrm{C}_2</math>, by defining <math>a</math> the identity element, and <math>bb = a</math>. Then it produces the following heap:

<math display=block>[a,a,a]=a,\, [a,a,b]=b,\, [b,a,a]=b,\, [b,a,b]=a,</math>
<math display=block>[a,b,a]=b,\, [a,b,b]=a,\, [b,b,a]=a,\, [b,b,b]=b.</math>

Defining <math>b</math> as the identity element and <math>aa = b</math> would have given the same heap.

=== Heap of integers ===
If <math>x,y,z</math> are integers, we can set <math>[x,y,z] = x-y+z</math> to produce a heap. We can then choose any [[integer]] <math>k</math> to be the identity of a new group on the set of integers, with the operation <math>*</math>
<math display=block>x*y = x+y-k</math>
and inverse
<math display=block>x^{-1} = 2k-x.</math>

=== Heap of a group ===
The previous two examples may be generalized to any group {{mvar|G}} by defining the ternary operation as <math>[x,y,z] = xy^{-1}z,</math> using the multiplication and inverse of {{mvar|G}}.

===Heap of a groupoid with two objects===
The heap of a group may be generalized again to the case of a [[groupoid]] which has two [[object (category theory)|objects]] {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}} when viewed as a [[category (mathematics)|category]]. The elements of the heap may be identified with the [[morphism]]s from A to B, such that three morphisms {{mvar|x}}, {{mvar|y}}, {{mvar|z}} define a heap operation according to <math>[x,y,z] = xy^{-1}z.</math>

This reduces to the heap of a group if a particular morphism between the two objects is chosen as the identity. This intuitively relates the description of isomorphisms between two objects as a heap and the description of isomorphisms between multiple objects as a groupoid.

===Heterogeneous relations===
Let {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}} be different sets and <math>\mathcal{B}(A,B)</math> the collection of [[heterogeneous relation]]s between them. For <math>p, q, r \in \mathcal{B}(A,B)</math> define the ternary operator
<math>[p, q, r] = p q^\mathrm{T} r</math> where {{math|''q''{{sup|T}}}} is the [[converse relation]] of {{mvar|q}}. The result of this composition is also in <math>\mathcal{B}(A,B)</math> so a mathematical structure has been formed by the ternary operation.<ref name=CH>Christopher Hollings (2014) ''Mathematics across the Iron Curtain: a history of the algebraic theory of semigroups'', pages 264,5, History of Mathematics 41, [[American Mathematical Society]] {{ISBN|978-1-4704-1493-1}}</ref> [[Viktor Wagner]] was motivated to form this heap by his study of transition maps in an [[atlas (topology)|atlas]] which are [[partial function]]s.<ref name=vagner1968>Vagner (1968)</ref> Thus a heap is more than a tweak of a group: it is a general concept including a group as a trivial case.

==Theorems==

{{Math theorem|A semiheap with a biunitary element {{mvar|e}} may be considered an [[Semigroup with involution|involuted semigroup]] with operation given by {{math|1=''ab'' = [''a'', ''e'', ''b'']}} and involution by {{math|1=''a''<sup>–1</sup> = [''e'', ''a'', ''e'']}}.<ref name=H&L/>{{rp|76}}}}

When the above construction is applied to a heap, the result is in fact a group.<ref name=H&L/>{{rp|143}} Note that the identity {{mvar|e}} of the group can be chosen to be any element of the heap.

{{Math theorem|Every semiheap may be embedded in an involuted semigroup.<ref name=H&L/>{{rp|78}}}}

As in the study of [[semigroup]]s, the structure of semiheaps is described in terms of [[semigroup ideal|ideal]]s with an "i-simple semiheap" being one with no proper ideals. Mustafaeva translated the [[Green's relations]] of semigroup theory to semiheaps and defined a &rho; class to be those elements generating the same principle two-sided ideal. He then proved that no i-simple semiheap can have more than two &rho; classes.<ref> L. G. Mustafaev (1966) "Ideal equivalences of semiheaps" {{mr|id=0202892}}</ref>

He also described regularity classes of a semiheap {{mvar|S}}:
<math display=block>D(m,n) = \{a \mid \exists x \in S : a = a^n x a^m \}</math> where {{mvar|n}} and {{mvar|m}} have the same [[parity (mathematics)|parity]] and the ternary operation of the semiheap applies at the left of a string from {{mvar|S}}.
He proves that {{mvar|S}} can have at most 5 regularity classes. Mustafaev calls an ideal {{mvar|B}} "isolated" when <math>a^n \in B \implies a \in B .</math> He then proves that when {{math|1=''S'' = D(2,2)}}, then every ideal is isolated and conversely.<ref>L. G. Mustafaev (1965) "Regularity classes of semiheaps" {{mr|id=0209386}}</ref>

Studying the semiheap {{math|Z(''A'', ''B'')}} of [[heterogeneous relation]]s between sets {{mvar|A}} and {{mvar|B}}, in 1974 K. A. Zareckii followed Mustafaev's lead to describe ideal equivalence, regularity classes, and ideal factors of a semiheap.<ref> K. A. Zareckii (1974) "Semiheaps of binary relations" {{mr|id=0364526}}</ref>

== Generalizations and related concepts ==

* A '''pseudoheap''' (or '''pseudogroud''') satisfies the partial para-associative condition<ref name=vagner1968>Vagner (1968)</ref> <math display=block>[[a,b,c],d,e] = [a,b,[c,d,e]] .</math>
* A '''Malcev operation''' satisfies the identity law but not necessarily the para-associative law,<ref>{{cite book |last1=Borceux|first1=Francis |last2=Bourn|first2=Dominique| title=Mal'cev, Protomodular, Homological and Semi-Abelian Categories| date=2004| url=https://books.google.com/books?id=olmeksCI22cC| publisher=Springer Science & Business Media|isbn=978-1-4020-1961-6}}</ref> that is, a [[ternary operation]] <math>f</math> on a set <math>X</math> satisfying the identity <math>f(x, x, y) = f(y, x, x) = y</math>. (See [[Congruence-permutable algebra]].)
* A '''semiheap''' (or '''semigroud''') is required to satisfy only the para-associative law but need not obey the identity law.<ref name=moldavska/><p>An example of a semiheap that is not in general a heap is given by {{mvar|M}} a [[ring (mathematics)|ring]] of [[matrix (mathematics)|matrices]] of fixed size with <math display="block">[x,y,z] = x \cdot y^\mathrm{T} \cdot z</math> where • denotes [[matrix multiplication]] and T denotes [[matrix transpose]].<ref name=moldavska>{{Cite journal | last=Moldavs'ka | first=Z. Ja. | title=Linear semiheaps | journal= Dopovidi Ahad. Nauk Ukrain. | series=RSR Ser. A | volume=1971 | pages=888–890, 957 |mr=297918}}</ref></p>
* An '''idempotent semiheap''' is a semiheap where <math> [a,a,a] = a </math> for all {{mvar|a}}.
* A '''generalised heap''' (or '''generalised groud''') is an idempotent semiheap where <math display="block">[a,a,[b,b,x]] = [b,b,[a,a,x]] </math> and <math display="block"> [[x,a,a],b,b] = [[x,b,b],a,a] </math> for all {{mvar|a}} and {{mvar|b}}.<p>In a semiheap, the relation → defined by <math display="block">a \rightarrow b \Leftrightarrow [a,b,a] = a </math> is [[transitive relation|transitive]]. A semiheap is a generalized heap if and only if → is an [[order relation]], that is, is also [[reflexive relation|reflexive]] (the semiheap is idempotent) and [[antisymmetric relation|antisymmetric]].<ref>Schein (1979) p.104</ref></p>
